verdict: Caution 71: grow with the units that are winning this shake-out, and stay away from those losing it.
now: Oct 2026 in Morbi: propane is above ₹100/kg, exports have nearly stopped, godowns are full and most units have cut output by 15–20%.

items.b: Energy is about 25–30% of production cost (BEE cluster profile); an older cluster study puts it at 30–35%. Kilns run on natural gas and spray dryers on coal.
A June 2025 broker note says fuel ‘should ideally be 25–30%’ of production cost but had risen to 35%, squeezing margins. Morbi burns about 7.3 mn SCM of gas a day.
Raw material (clay, feldspar, zirconium silicate, glaze) and fuel are the two main cost heads (ICRA). Collect the split for labour, power, packing and freight from the customer.

Low entry barriers and many unorganised players limit price rises, so cost spikes hit margins first. In one Morbi sanitaryware firm, operating margin fell from 17% (FY18) to 13% (FY22) on gas and input costs. In 2026 Morbi players took 30–40% price hikes as gas rose, sharply narrowing their discount to branded tiles.

items.h: Cash is locked in stock and dealers
items.b: Making many designs means heavy finished-goods stock, and dealers get long credit. One rated Morbi group had gross current asset days of 204 and operating cycle days of 145 (FY24). Asian Granito gives dealers up to 90 days, gets up to 120 days from suppliers and holds 45–60 days of stock.
Rated Morbi units show average working-capital utilisation of 84–86% and NWC/OI of 30–48%.
Kilns, presses and polishing lines are capital-heavy, but no source here gives a cost per line. Collect project cost and capacity from the customer.
Propane up ₹7,300/tonne, now above ₹100/kg, adding about ₹6/m³ → margin falls because price rises lag (weak pricing power) → lower cash accruals against fixed instalments.
Middle East war and container shortage → exports nearly stopped, godowns full → cash tied up in stock → cash credit drawn to the top.
Most units have cut output 15–20% → fixed costs (interest, salaries, minimum gas offtake) are spread over fewer boxes → lower DSCR.

In Wankaner, four men were booked for allegedly demanding ₹35 lakh on a ₹10 lakh loan to a ceramics labour contractor. This is a sign that money is tight in the cluster and private moneylenders are active.

sections.t: What to check in the papers
sections.note: Analytical framing: what to look for, not data. Set the limits under your credit policy.

items.h: P&L: power & fuel as % of sales
items.b: Compare the last 2–3 quarters with last year. Bad reading: rising while realisation per box is flat.
Inventory days now vs same month last year. Bad reading: sharp rise, or finished goods growing faster than sales.
Share above 90 days (Asian Granito's normal credit is up to 90). Bad reading: growing tail, or the same dealers rolling over.

items.h: GSTR-1 vs GSTR-3B vs bank credits
items.b: Bad reading: GST turnover well above credits into the account, or a drop in zero-rated (export) supplies in GSTR-1 with no rise in domestic sales.
Utilisation compared with the 84–86% seen in rated peers. Bad reading: stuck near the limit for months, or month-end round-tripping.
Bad reading: inward or outward cheque returns, or cash or third-party credits matching ‘unsecured loans’.
Monthly SCM consumed vs last year shows true production. Bad reading: consumption down while the stock statement shows rising output.
How many days a month is each kiln firing? Is any line shut? Ask to see the kiln log.
Count stock by size and design against the latest stock statement. Look at dust and old batch dates on boxes.
See the last 3 Gujarat Gas bills: rate, SCM and any arrears. Is the unit getting the ₹5/SCM relief?
Top 10 dealers and their dues. Has any dealer stopped lifting stock? What is the export share, and are any export orders stuck?
Headcount now vs the wage register, and whether contractor payments are on time.
Any loans from family, friends or private moneylenders? How much capital has come in or gone out this year?

signals.issue: A shake-out: weaker units close and dealers' dues to them become hard to collect, while survivors gain volume.
signals.guard: Back units with a domestic dealer base and promoter liquidity. For export-heavy units, cap working capital to actual dispatches and tie limits to a monthly drawing-power review.

title: Morbi tiles: a note to the credit manager
narrative: ## Start with what the business is

A Morbi tile unit takes clay, feldspar and glaze, presses them, and fires them in a long gas kiln. Out come square metres of tile in boxes. The product is close to a commodity, and buyers move for a few rupees, so **the unit wins on cost per sqm and on reaching dealers, not on brand.**

Fuel is the cost that swings. Energy is normally **25–30% of production cost** [6]. One broker note says it had already crept to **35%** by mid-2025 [8]. Raw material and fuel are the two big cost heads [9]. Collect the split for labour, power, packing and freight from the customer. Do not assume it.
## Where the cash goes

Cash does not sit in the plant. It sits in stock and with dealers. Units make many designs, so finished stock piles up, and dealers expect credit [10]. One rated Morbi group ran **204 gross current asset days** in FY24 [10]. Asian Granito gives dealers up to **90 days** and holds **45–60 days** of stock [11]. Rated Morbi units show working-capital limits **84–86% used** on average [9][10].

**So when a proposal lands, read the stock statement before the P&L.** If finished goods are growing faster than sales, the unit is making to stock and funding it with your CC. Ask for stock by size and design, and its age.
## What broke this year

Gas, then exports. Morbi was **shut from end-March to mid-May** on gas scarcity [21]. Gas went from **₹50 on 28 Feb to ₹91** now, per Kajaria's chairman [16]. On 22 Oct propane rose **₹7,300 a tonne**, crossing **₹100/kg** [3][4], and its discount to natural gas is down to about **5%** [15]. Units that switched to propane to save money have lost that cushion.

Exports, normally a safety valve, have closed. Cluster exports fell to **~₹2,900 cr in Q1 FY27 from ~₹4,800 cr**, with volumes **down 51%** [18]. In Oct the Ceramic Association said exports are nearly stopped, godowns are full and most units have cut output **15–20%** [3]. Kajaria's chairman puts **40–50% of Morbi's ~400–500 plants** as not working [16]. The two numbers measure different things, so ask your borrower which camp it is in, and verify it from kiln running days and its Gujarat Gas SCM consumption.

The chain to repayment is short. A higher gas bill comes first, then a price rise that may not stick, then unsold stock, then CC stuck at the limit, then pressure on instalments. **Morbi players did push 30–40% price hikes this year** [19][16]. The question is whether their buyers keep paying.
## Why there is growth here

This is a shake-out, and shake-outs create winners. The price gap between Morbi and branded tiles has narrowed from about **₹800 to ₹50–55** [21], and dealers are spreading their buying beyond Morbi [21]. Branded players are taking share. Kajaria grew volume **10%**, its tile realisation rose **11.4%** and its EBITDA margin is **19.51%** [13][15]. Somany's tile realisation is up **20.3% to ₹384/sqm** [19]. Somany also warns that about **200 more Morbi units** may shut if price hikes don't hold [17].
**The units to pursue now:**

- Units that make for, or supply, branded players. Somany buys about **32%** of its sales from outsourcing partners [19], and Kajaria cites Morbi plants and outsourced volumes [16]. A unit with a named offtaker has the most visible cash flow in the cluster.
- Domestic dealer-led units with a spread-out network and low export share, as shown in GSTR-1.
- Efficient, modern kilns with low gas per sqm. Collect SCM per sqm from the customer and compare it within your own book.
- Strong survivors buying capacity from units that have shut, at sensible valuations.
## How to grow it safely

Size working capital to dispatches, not to capacity. Take the monthly Gujarat Gas bill with every stock statement, because SCM consumed is the most honest production figure a tile unit has. If the stock statement says production is up and the gas bill says down, believe the gas bill. Stress-test DSCR at today's gas cost with no further price hike. For term loans on new lines, make sure the promoter brings real equity. Kajaria itself just raised its own project cost estimate from **₹210 cr to ₹340 cr** [15], so capex overruns are live risk.

For an export-heavy unit, ask for month-wise export vs domestic sales for Apr–Sep 2026 from GSTR-1. Treat stock made before June as slow-moving when you compute drawing power. Earlier, in the Red Sea disruption, one rated Morbi group's cash from operations fell from **₹42.20 cr to ₹14.47 cr** as stock built up on delayed export orders [10]. **Stock builds first and profit falls later. Read cash flow, not PAT.**
## Spotting trouble early

The first signs show up in the bank account before the balance sheet. Watch for CC pinned at the limit month after month, inward cheque returns, and third-party or cash credits booked as unsecured loans. On site, a cold kiln, dusty boxes with old batch dates, and a thinner labour roll tell you more than the CMA. Informal money is in the cluster: in Wankaner four men were booked for allegedly extorting **₹35 lakh on a ₹10 lakh loan** to a ceramics labour contractor [2]. Ask the promoter plainly about private borrowing, and match the answer to the bank statement.

Gas arrears or a disconnection notice means production can stop overnight. Treat it like an overdue. A stock statement that doesn't match the godown means the drawing power is fiction: stop fresh drawals until it is reconciled.

Below the same month last year for 3 months → review limits for export-heavy units.
Pinned at the limit for 3 months, or any return → SMA watch and promoter meeting.
